content: Tyrothricin is a mixture of cyclic polypeptide antibiotics derived from Bacillus brevis. It is an antibiotic that is effective against gram-positive bacteria and is typically used for localized applications. It is sometimes combined with 5 mg of benzocaine to provide symptomatic relief for sore throats. However, systemic absorption of tyrothricin can result in severe adverse effects, which is why its use is restricted to topical applications. Tyrothricin belongs to the pharmacological class of polypeptide antibiotics, which also includes colistin, polymyxin B, and bacitracin. Importantly, there is no cross-resistance between tyrothricin and these other agents. Tyrothricin exerts its antibacterial effects by inhibiting protein biosynthesis in gram-positive organisms. However, it is completely ineffective against gram-negative bacteria. The primary indications for tyrothricin include inflammation of the throat, gastric mucosa, and angina tonsillaris. It is essential that the mucous membrane remains intact during its use to prevent tyrothricin from entering the bloodstream, thereby minimizing the risk of systemic absorption and associated side effects. Known side effects of tyrothricin include hypersensitivity reactions, temporary disturbances in balance (related to the vestibular system), and nephrotoxic effects, such as impaired renal function. There is currently no long-term data available regarding its safety during pregnancy or lactation. Tyrothricin is marketed under various trade names. As a standalone preparation, it is sold as Limexx (Austria) and Tyrosur (Germany). In combination formulations, it is available as Citropain (Switzerland), Dorithricin (Germany, Austria), Lemocin (Germany, Austria, Switzerland), Mebucaine (Switzerland), Mebucasol (Switzerland), Otothricinol (Switzerland), Sangerol (Switzerland), Solmucaine (Switzerland), Trachisan (Germany), Tyroqualin (Switzerland), and Tyrozets (United Kingdom). Generic versions are also available in Austria and Switzerland.
